1) The provision of family‐centred comprehensive primary care for HIV‐infected adults and their children is a feasible and desirable strategy to improve health and quality of life in resource‐limited areas.

a comprehensive, family‐ centred service package for primary care in resource‐limited HIV/AIDS programs is feasible and acceptable, and that it improves the health and well‐being of HIV‐infected adults and their family members.
A family‐centred, comprehensive, primary care package for adults, adolescents, children, and families with HIV/AIDS is feasible and effective.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How can a package of primary health services be designed that can effectively be delivered to HIV‐infected families in low‐resource settings?
the development of a package of primary care services to support comprehensive HIV/AIDS family care and treatment programmes in resource‐limited countries.
the development of a service package for the comprehensive family‐centric care of HIV/AIDS in resource limited settings.

the package of primary care services described here is a useful tool to help programs in resource‐limited setting to develop comprehensive family‐centres care for HIV/AIDS.
the evidence supports a package of primary health services for HIV/AIDS patients in resource‐constrained settings.
a package of primary health services for family‐centred comprehensive family‐centres care is a useful tool for program designers in resource limited settings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the family‐centred approach to care is the best approach to care in resource‐limited setting.
the family‐centred approach to HIV/AIDS is a promising strategy that has the potential to improve the health of people living with HIV/AIDS, their families, and their communities.
we are developing and testing an integrated family‐centred service package for the management of HIV/AIDS in low‐income countries.
The main takeaway from our work is that

comprehensive, family‐centered care is possible in resource‐limited countries, but that the implementation of such care requires careful planning and the use of existing resources to their maximum potential.

a package of primary care services for HIV care and treatment programs can be developed and that such a package should be based upon evidence from both high‐income and low‐ and middle‐income countries.
a comprehensive, family‐centered approach to HIV/AIDS care and prevention can improve health outcomes for patients in resource‐limited countries.
